**My reasoning:**

I'm 61. I've been farming this land since I was a young man, watching my father do the same. Here in Quzhou, everyone grows wheat in the winter and maize in the summer on the same land. That's how it works on the North China Plain — you don't change what works.

I have about 10 mu of flat land. After the wheat harvest in June, I'll turn around and plant maize on that same ground before the rains come. I don't need to think hard about this — it's what I know, it's what the market wants, and it's what the grain buyers in town will take.

For wheat, I'll use the Kenong 199 variety that my neighbor has been using — it's a good improved line, not too fancy, I can buy the seed from the county supply cooperative. For maize, Zhengdan 958. I've used it for years. It doesn't fail me.

I water wheat four times — before winter freeze, at jointing, at heading, and when the grain is filling. Water is what wheat needs here, the rain doesn't come until summer. For maize the summer rains usually help but I'll pump once to be safe if July is dry.

I put down plenty of fertilizer. More is safer than less — a bad harvest means a bad year. I spread base fertilizer before planting wheat and top-dress urea in spring. For maize I apply at planting and side-dress when it's knee high.

I spray pesticides when I see problems starting — aphids on the wheat in May, herbicide on the maize soon after emergence. My son sometimes helps with the spraying since my back isn't what it was.

I use rotary tillage before wheat planting — it's easier on my tractor and handles the maize stubble fine.
